name: Glitch Art
visualIdentity: Digital signal failure made deliberate: brief strip offsets, RGB separation, block damage, and reconstruction interrupt a clear image, then restore it. Establish a fault model such as signal loss or displacement; avoid continuous random corruption. The style has no intrinsic palette.
suitableUses: Explicitly: short, transition-led edits and hybrids where a fault interrupts meaningful content, such as kinetic typography or a system interface. It can suit tech promotions, security explainers, and abrasive digital transitions. Suitability for video or interactive HTML depends on keeping the subject and message legible.
limitations: Avoid calm editorial scenes and distortion that obscures communication. Glitch only elements implicated by the story; body copy and most of the runtime should remain clean. Use bounded events with readable endpoints, prompt restoration, and no rapid flashing. Do not use when chapter changes obscure causality or violate a continuous-shot or loop requirement.
palette: No canonical colors are specified. Preserve task, brand, reference, and source-asset colors and their roles; intentional signal faults are the stated exception. Optional fallback tokens for new presentation elements only: background #111A24, foreground #F2F0E6, accents #47B3AF and #D16A84. Keep these four discrete colors; gradients are disabled. Never recolor source imagery. Suggested opaque text pairs meet 4.5:1, but contrast must be checked on actual composites.
motionAndInteraction: Use timed displacement, channel separation, and localized damage, then restore the clean source after each event. Video state must be deterministic and seekable. For HTML, bounded scroll progress can scrub a glitch cut reversibly; keyboard navigation and reduced-motion cuts are supported. A headline may glitch once on hover or focus, with selectable text. Keep endpoints readable and avoid flashing.
audio: No fixed soundtrack or mandatory layer. Choose music, narration, vocals, effects, ambience, or silence for the topic and explicit audio requirements. Glitch transitions may use restrained accents, but leave room for speech and comprehension. Audio assets are selected separately, then synchronized and mixed with picture; verify intelligibility, balance, clipping, and sync.
assetRequirements: Use supplied or authorized assets and exact copy; preserve source artwork and asset colors. Inspect actual imagery before choosing damage targets. Prepare and cache stateful simulations; seed randomness and drive visuals from shared composition time. Missing assets and unverified limits should be reported, not invented.
combinations: Glitch Art alone suits short transition-led edits. Kinetic typography (style-093) provides a clean baseline for brief faults; a HUD/interface (style-112) can make a specific system failure the narrative event. Limit damage to the named text or panels, restore clarity, and avoid clutter. Other compatible abrasive styles are listed, but require scene-level review.
productionApproach: Use WebGL and GLSL for procedural displacement and channel-separation passes; use timed localized damage and restore the source. These own visual rendering and motion. HyperFrames is the primary video assembly, timing, sync, validation, and export pipeline; use Remotion only if unavailable or a verified limitation blocks a required capability, documenting why. For HTML, use deterministic bounded progress and suitable DOM/CSS or shader layers. Keep one owner per animated property. Inspect representative frames, seeks, decoded output, and audio; deliver editable source, contact sheet, parameters, and reproducible render instructions.
